newsitem.title: USA: HORSE RACING-INTERNATIONAL BUYERS BOOST YEARLING SALES.
newsitem.headline: HORSE RACING-INTERNATIONAL BUYERS BOOST YEARLING SALES.

text.p: Prices for premiere yearlings rose sharply at the opening session of Keeneland's July Selected Yearling Sale Monday, reflecting a record-breaking stock market and stable interest rates.
International buyers from Ireland, England, Japan and Dubai continued to dominate sales as they have in recent years.
Demi O'Byrne, an Irish veterinarian, bought the sales topper, a chestnut filly by Gulch out of Sabin, for $1,050,000 for Coolmore Stud, Ireland, whose principals are Michael Tabor and John Magnier.
O'Byrne, as agent, spent $6,900,000 on ten yearlings by such legendary stallions as Danzig, Nureyev, Storm Cat
Darley Stud and Shadwell Estate, buying for Sheikhs Mohammed and Akmed of the ruling family of Dubai, purchased horses for $4,820,000 including colts by Mr. Prospector, Woodman, Danzig.
A record number of 82 Japanese individuals, represented by 12 groups, were active buyers in the mid-price range, around $200,000, but did not go after the high-ticket horses.
The average price was $367,582 compared to $299,136 last year. The median was $300,000 compared to $250,000 last year.

Two Americans battled each other for the brown filly by Gone West out of Finezza. The bidding war was won by D. Wayne Lukas, agent and trainer, for $450,000. Bloodstock agent Patrick Lawley-Wakelin of Middleburg, Virgina, lost out.

"Right now, it's hard to find value because the prices for the right horses are a lot higher than last year. The horses' conformation has been exceptional, matching their pedigree, and the prices seem to match. We haven't bought anything tonight," Lawley-Wakelin explained.

But the market seemed to be forking in two different directions. While prices were up, so were the numbers of RNA's -- Reserve Not Attained, where a consignor takes a horse back because the reserve price was not met. Thirty-four horses were RNA's from the opening sale of 130 head.

"The filly market was stronger than people expected. There's a shortage on the commercial market. People tend to to keep them," explained W. B. Rogers Beasley, Keeneland's director of sales. He also predicted the first session would be the strongest of this year's sales.
The second and final session is Tuesday night.
